name: Heaptrack
workload: Heap allocation profiling of arbitrary Linux applications, time and memory overhead versus Massif.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: overhead in both time and memory significantly lower than Massif; multi-threaded apps are not serialized.
tradeoffs: Cannot profile stack allocations or pool allocators that bypass malloc (Massif can); Linux only; preloads an allocator-interposing library.
caveats: README claim has no numbers. License SPDX id is inferred: repo page showed a LICENSES directory with several files, individual identifiers not read. Author blog (milianw.de) was egress-blocked.
found_via: WebSearch: heaptrack faster than Valgrind massif overhead comparison

name: wallClockProfiler
workload: Profiling overhead on the author's own test program (fseek-bound), wall-clock stack sampling via GDB.
claimed_speedup: About 12% slowdown at 20 samples/second versus callgrind about 11x slowdown (160 s versus 14 s).
tradeoffs: Samples through GDB so each sample stops the process; wall-clock sampling shows I/O waits that CPU-cycle profilers miss.
caveats: Single synthetic test program, no hardware or compiler stated, only first-party. Overhead of the two tools differs by design (sampling rate versus exact tracing). Public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
found_via: WebSearch: github sampling profiler README faster than callgrind gprof perf overhead

name: Dr. Memory
workload: Memory error detection (uninitialized reads, overflows, use-after-free, leaks) on SPEC CPU 2006 on Linux.
claimed_speedup: README: faster than Valgrind on SPECCPU2006 per the CGO 2011 paper, and Valgrind cannot run 434.zeusmp and 447.dealII. Google sanitizers comparison page lists about 10x slowdown for Dr. Memory versus about 20x for Memcheck.
tradeoffs: Built on DynamoRIO; still a dynamic binary instrumentation tool so slowdown stays several times native; Windows, Linux, Mac, Android.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (CGO 2011) could not be opened (host blocked); numbers come from the README claim and the sanitizers wiki page, which lacks hardware and compiler. License listed as LGPL on the repo page, version not confirmed. Tier B rests on the paper.
found_via: WebSearch: Valgrind alternative faster dynamic binary instrumentation memory error detector

name: AddressSanitizer (google/sanitizers)
workload: Memory error detection overhead, compile-time instrumentation versus dynamic binary instrumentation; SPEC CPU 2006 for ASan alone.
claimed_speedup: Comparison page: ASan 2x slowdown versus Valgrind/Memcheck 20x and Dr. Memory 10x. Performance page: average slowdown 1.93, median 1.86 on SPEC CPU 2006.
compiler_and_flags: clang 3.3 trunk r179094, -O2 -fsanitize=address, frame pointers on (SPEC numbers page)
stars_or_usage: 12.5k stars; shipped in LLVM and GCC
tradeoffs: Needs recompilation; no uninitialized-read detection (use MemorySanitizer); about 2x memory.
caveats: Repo archived, core code lives in LLVM compiler-rt. The Valgrind comparison table is first-party, rounded, and gives no hardware or compiler; hardware and compiler above belong to the separate SPEC page with no Valgrind column. Numbers date from 2013. License is the LLVM project license, not read from this repo page. Canonical code repo is llvm/llvm-project.
found_via: WebSearch: Valgrind alternative much faster ... memory error detector; page google/sanitizers wiki

name: DoubleTake
workload: Evidence-based detection of heap overflows, use-after-free and leaks, runtime overhead on benchmark suites.
claimed_speedup: About 2% runtime overhead for buffer overflow detection, stated as substantially lower than Valgrind and AddressSanitizer.
tradeoffs: Detects errors after the fact via checkpoint and replay; needs deterministic replay, so programs with external I/O are harder; Linux.
caveats: Number is from the README summary of an academic paper (arXiv 1601.07962, not opened: arXiv blocked); only the overflow-detection configuration is quoted. Peer-review status not verified.
found_via: WebSearch: Valgrind alternative much faster dynamic binary instrumentation

name: Bytehound
workload: Allocation tracing with stack traces on Linux.
claimed_speedup: README says its custom stack unwinding is a lot cheaper than other similar tools, potentially up to orders of magnitude, no figures.
tradeoffs: Linux only, LD_PRELOAD; usable from C++ programs as a preload library but implemented in Rust.
caveats: No numbers, baseline tools not named in the quoted claim. Tier D kept as notable (4.8k stars).
